items.title: Gifts, hospitality and conflicts of interest (level 4)
items.source: Civil Service Code; Civil Service Management Code
items.body: The Civil Service Code says civil servants must not accept gifts or hospitality, or any other benefit, that might be seen to influence their judgement. The test is not only whether you are influenced but whether others could reasonably think so. Each department has its own gifts and hospitality policy and usually a register. Typical rules are that low-value items such as a diary or a box of biscuits from a customer may be accepted openly or shared with the team, while anything more valuable, or anything offered by a company that is bidding for a contract, must be declined or reported to a manager. Cash is never acceptable. Offers should be recorded in the register even when they are declined. A conflict of interest is a situation in which your private interests, or those of family and close friends, could affect, or appear to affect, your official duties. Examples are handling the claim of a relative, taking part in choosing a supplier owned by a friend, or having a second job that overlaps with your work. A conflict does not mean you have done anything wrong, but it must be declared as soon as you spot it. The manager will then decide what to do, which often means giving the work to someone else. Failing to declare a conflict is more serious than having one.

questions.prompt: A supplier bidding for a department contract sends you an expensive bottle of wine. What is the right response?

options.text: Accept it because it was not offered for a particular favour
Decline it politely and record the offer in the register
Keep it, but return the favour when the contract is awarded
Accept it and put it in the team's shared fridge for later

questions.hint: Gifts from bidders could be seen to influence judgement, so they are declined and recorded.

questions.prompt: Which of these is the test for whether a gift may be accepted?

options.text: Whether others could reasonably think it might influence your judgement
Whether you personally feel that it would change your decisions
Whether the gift was wrapped and sent to the office address rather than home
Whether the giver is a member of the public or a company

questions.hint: The test covers how a gift might reasonably appear, not only how you feel.

questions.prompt: Why should an offer be recorded in the register even when it was declined?

options.text: It gives the offered gift to the team to share later
It lets the person who made the offer know that it has been written down
It shows the department that the offer was made and handled openly
It allows the civil servant to claim the value as expenses

questions.hint: Recording offers keeps the process open and transparent.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a conflict of interest?

options.text: Being asked to cover a team member who is on leave
Disagreeing with a colleague about how to apply a rule
Being asked to process a claim made by your own sister
Being given a claim that is longer than your usual cases

questions.hint: Handling a relative's claim mixes private and official duties.

questions.prompt: When should a conflict of interest be declared?

options.text: Only if a customer or colleague points it out
As soon as you become aware of it
After you have finished the work involved
Once a year during your appraisal

questions.hint: Declaring early lets the manager arrange for someone else to take over.

questions.prompt: What often happens after a conflict of interest has been declared?

options.text: The civil servant must repay the value of the work
The customer must apply to a different department
The manager arranges for the work to be done by someone else
The civil servant is moved out of the department as a disciplinary step

questions.hint: Managers usually reallocate the work.

questions.prompt: Which is more serious in relation to conflicts of interest?

options.text: Moving a case to a colleague at your own request
Failing to declare one that you knew about
Declaring one that turned out to be minor
Asking your manager whether something counts

questions.hint: Hiding a known conflict breaks integrity.

questions.prompt: A customer leaves cash as a thank-you at the counter. What should you do?

options.text: Refuse it and tell your manager what happened
Put it in the office charity box without telling anyone
Accept it if the amount is very small
Keep it for the team's next social event

questions.hint: Cash is never acceptable and should be reported.

items.title: Raising concerns and protection for whistleblowers (level 4)
items.source: Civil Service Code; Public Interest Disclosure Act 1998
items.body: Raising a concern means telling someone that you think something wrong is happening at work. The Civil Service Code sets out the route. If you are asked to act in a way you believe is illegal, improper, unethical or in breach of constitutional conventions, or if you see something that worries you, you should first report it to your line manager or another manager in the department. Your department also has a nominated officer, who can be approached in confidence. Many departments run a whistleblowing helpline too. If the concern is not resolved to your satisfaction, you can take it to the Civil Service Commission, which can investigate. Where the matter involves criminal or unlawful activity, the Code expects you to report it to the police or other appropriate authority. The Public Interest Disclosure Act 1998 protects workers who make a disclosure in good faith, in the public interest, in the proper way. A worker who is punished for such a disclosure, for example by being dismissed or demoted, can bring a claim at an employment tribunal. Protection depends on using the right channel, so it is best to follow your department's policy and take advice from the nominated officer before going outside the organisation. Do not investigate the matter yourself, and do not accuse anyone, but report what you saw and when.

questions.prompt: You see a colleague changing the amount on a payment to benefit a friend. What should you do first?

options.text: Post a warning about it on the staff intranet
Confront the colleague in front of the rest of the team and demand an answer
Report what you saw to your line manager or the nominated officer
Change the payment back and say nothing to anyone

questions.hint: The Code says to report concerns to a manager or nominated officer.

questions.prompt: What is the role of a nominated officer?

options.text: To decide for the department whether or not the concern is true
To receive concerns in confidence from staff in the department
To represent staff in disciplinary meetings
To investigate crimes on behalf of the police

questions.hint: Nominated officers are a confidential route for concerns.

questions.prompt: Which external body can investigate a concern that remains unresolved?

options.text: The Civil Service Commission
The Health and Safety Executive
The Equality and Human Rights Commission
The Information Commissioner's Office

questions.hint: The Commission can investigate unresolved Code concerns.

questions.prompt: Where does the Code say evidence of criminal activity should be reported?

options.text: To the National Audit Office only
To the police or another appropriate authority
To the department's press office
To the Prime Minister's private office at 10 Downing Street

questions.hint: The Code points to the police or other proper authorities.

questions.prompt: What does the Public Interest Disclosure Act 1998 do?

options.text: Requires all workers to report any concerns within one week of first seeing them
Gives workers the right to see their manager's records
Protects workers who raise concerns in the public interest in good faith
Stops employers from investigating workers' concerns

questions.hint: The Act protects whistleblowers from unfair treatment.

questions.prompt: A worker is demoted after raising a genuine concern properly. What can they do?

options.text: Bring a claim at an employment tribunal
Apply to the Cabinet Secretary for a new post
Ask the Prime Minister to overturn the decision
Ask Parliament to vote on the demotion

questions.hint: The Act allows claims at a tribunal.

questions.prompt: Why is it better to follow the department's policy before going outside the organisation?

options.text: The department will pay you a reward
Outside bodies are not allowed to hear concerns
Going outside is a criminal offence in all cases
Protection depends on using the right channel

questions.hint: Using the proper route helps keep legal protection.

questions.prompt: Which of these should you avoid when you have a concern?

options.text: Writing down what you saw, when it happened and who else was there
Investigating the matter yourself and accusing someone
Asking the nominated officer for advice
Reporting it as soon as you can

questions.hint: You should report what you saw, not play detective.

items.title: Political activity and the rules for different grades (level 4)
items.source: Civil Service Management Code; Civil Service Code
items.body: Civil servants are citizens as well as officials, and they keep many of their rights. They can vote, hold political opinions, and join a political party. The rules limit what they can do publicly so that ministers and the public can trust that the Civil Service is impartial. The Civil Service Management Code sets out the rules and puts staff in broad groups. The most senior grades, including the Senior Civil Service and Grades 6 and 7, and certain other staff, are politically restricted. They may not take part in national political activity, such as standing for Parliament or speaking publicly on behalf of a party. Most other staff are in a middle group and may take part in some activities with permission, but should not take part in local political activity in the area where they work if it could affect their job. A small group of industrial and non-office grades are politically free. Any civil servant who wants to stand for election to Parliament must resign first. A civil servant who is a member of a party, or who wants to do something political such as canvassing, helping at a campaign or standing as a councillor, should speak to their manager or HR first, because the rules depend on the role. During an election period, extra care is expected, and official time, equipment and information must never be used for party political purposes.

questions.prompt: Which statement about civil servants and political parties is correct?

options.text: They may hold political opinions, but there are limits on public activity
They are required to stay out of all politics during their working life
They are required to join and campaign for the party that is currently in government
They are banned from voting in general elections

questions.hint: Civil servants keep their political opinions and their vote.

questions.prompt: Which group is politically restricted?

options.text: The Senior Civil Service and Grades 6 and 7
Executive Officers and Higher Executive Officers
Staff who work part time
Administrative Assistants and Administrative Officers

questions.hint: Senior grades face the tightest limits.

questions.prompt: What must a civil servant do before standing for election to the House of Commons?

options.text: Resign from the Civil Service
Ask the Prime Minister for permission
Take a year's unpaid leave
Move to a different department

questions.hint: Candidates for Parliament must leave the Civil Service.

questions.prompt: An AO wants to help at a local candidate's campaign at weekends. What should they do?

options.text: Wait until the election is over before mentioning it to anyone at work
Go ahead, because weekends are private time
Tell only the candidate that they work in the Civil Service
Check the rules with their manager or HR before getting involved

questions.hint: The rules depend on the role and the activity.

questions.prompt: Which of these breaks the rules whatever the grade?

options.text: Discussing the news with family at home
Reading a party's manifesto document on your own phone at home
Using a work computer to print leaflets for a party
Voting in a local council election

questions.hint: Official equipment must never be used for party politics.

questions.prompt: Why are the rules on public political activity needed?

options.text: So that senior staff can avoid paying taxes
So that civil servants can concentrate on policy rather than service delivery
So that only one party can employ civil servants
So that ministers and the public can trust civil servants to be impartial

questions.hint: The rules protect trust in impartiality.

questions.prompt: Which document sets out the rules on political activity?

options.text: The Cabinet Manual published by the Cabinet Office
The Recruitment Principles
The Cabinet Manual
The Civil Service Management Code

questions.hint: The Management Code covers political activity.

questions.prompt: Who is in the politically free group?

options.text: Every member of the Fast Stream
All new starters
All staff at Executive Officer grade and above in London offices
A small group of industrial and non-office staff

questions.hint: Only a small group is politically free.

items.title: Giving advice and carrying out decisions (level 4)
items.source: Civil Service Code; Managing Public Money; GOV.UK
items.body: A central idea in the Civil Service is that civil servants give advice honestly, and then carry out decisions loyally. Civil servants advise ministers by setting out the evidence, the options, the costs and the risks. They should do so even when the advice is unwelcome, and they should not tell ministers only what they want to hear. This is sometimes called speaking truth to power. Once the minister has made a decision, within the law and the Code, the civil servants must put it into effect with full commitment. The Code says civil servants must not frustrate the implementation of policies once decisions are taken, by declining to take or abusing their power to take action. In rare cases a civil servant may believe an instruction is wrong. The rule then is to raise the concern with the line manager, and if necessary the nominated officer and Civil Service Commission. Accounting Officers have a particular duty. If they think a spending plan breaks the tests of regularity, propriety, value for money or feasibility, they can ask for a written instruction from the minister, called a ministerial direction. The minister then takes responsibility, and the department follows the direction. Each of these rules protects the public, because it makes sure decisions are taken with the facts in front of the decision maker, and are then delivered properly.

questions.prompt: A team is asked to brief a minister on a plan with a serious risk. What should the briefing include?

options.text: The risk, set out plainly alongside the other evidence
The risk, but only if the minister asks about it
The risk, in a note sent to the press office instead
Only the benefits, so that the minister is not discouraged by the risk

questions.hint: Honest advice includes unwelcome facts.

questions.prompt: What does the phrase speaking truth to power describe?

options.text: Giving ministers honest advice even when it is unwelcome
Telling the public about decisions before the minister does
Refusing to carry out a policy you disagree with
Challenging every decision a minister takes

questions.hint: Honest advice is a core duty.

questions.prompt: After a lawful decision is made, what does the Code say a civil servant must not do?

options.text: Ask for the decision to be confirmed in writing
Keep a written record of the advice that they gave to the minister before the decision
Frustrate the policy by declining to act or abusing their power to act
Tell the minister the risks of the policy

questions.hint: The Code bans frustrating the implementation of policy.

questions.prompt: A civil servant thinks an instruction is unlawful. What is the right step?

options.text: Raise the concern with their line manager or nominated officer
Carry out the instruction and tell the press afterwards
Ask the Opposition to look into it
Quietly ignore the instruction and carry on with other work instead

questions.hint: The Code provides a route for raising concerns.

questions.prompt: What is a ministerial direction?

options.text: A letter from a minister to all staff, thanking them for delivering a new policy
A minister's written order after an Accounting Officer objects to spending
A leaflet explaining a new policy to the public
A job description for a ministerial adviser

questions.hint: It transfers responsibility for the decision to the minister.

questions.prompt: Which test is NOT one an Accounting Officer applies to a spending plan?

options.text: Popularity with the public
Value for money
Propriety
Regularity, meaning spending within the law and the limits Parliament set

questions.hint: Popularity is not one of the tests.

questions.prompt: Why do these rules protect the public?

options.text: Decisions are made with the facts in front of the decision maker
They give civil servants the final say on policy
They keep policy secret until it has been delivered
They stop ministers from making decisions without a vote in Parliament

questions.hint: Advice and delivery together protect the public.

questions.prompt: Which person best shows the right balance of challenge and loyalty?

options.text: A civil servant who delivers every decision without advice
A civil servant who publicly criticises decisions they dislike
A civil servant who gives honest advice, then delivers the lawful decision
A civil servant who delays delivering decisions until they personally agree with them

questions.hint: Honest advice followed by full delivery is the right model.

items.title: How a department is organised (level 4)
items.source: GOV.UK, Departments, agencies and public bodies; Civil Service Jobs
items.body: Every department has a similar shape. At the top is the Secretary of State, the senior minister who is responsible to Parliament for the department. They are supported by junior ministers, usually called Ministers of State and Parliamentary Under-Secretaries of State, who look after parts of the department's work. The most senior civil servant is the Permanent Secretary, who runs the department day to day, advises the Secretary of State, and is the Accounting Officer. Below them are Directors General, who lead large groups of work, and Directors and Deputy Directors, who lead smaller areas. Together these are in the Senior Civil Service. Below the Senior Civil Service the grades continue from Grade 6 and Grade 7 down to Senior Executive Officer, Higher Executive Officer, Executive Officer, Administrative Officer and Administrative Assistant. Most departments also have a board, made up of senior civil servants and non-executive directors from outside government, who give advice and challenge on how the department is run. Non-executive directors are not civil servants, and they bring experience from business and other sectors. Each department is divided into groups, directorates and teams. A new AO will usually join a team of around a dozen or so people led by an EO or HEO, within a directorate and a group. Knowing where your team fits helps you understand who makes which decisions.

questions.prompt: Who is responsible to Parliament for a department as a whole?

options.text: The Permanent Secretary
The Director General
The Secretary of State
The Cabinet Secretary

questions.hint: The Secretary of State is the senior minister.

questions.prompt: Which role is the Accounting Officer in a department?

options.text: The Minister of State
The Secretary of State
The Permanent Secretary
The Chief Executive of an agency

questions.hint: The Permanent Secretary is the Accounting Officer.

questions.prompt: What do Ministers of State and Parliamentary Under-Secretaries of State do?

options.text: Audit the department's accounts on behalf of the National Audit Office
Run the department on a day-to-day basis as civil servants
Sit on the board as non-executive directors
Look after parts of the department's work as junior ministers

questions.hint: They are junior ministers.

questions.prompt: Where does the Senior Civil Service begin?

options.text: At Deputy Director level
At Grade 7
At Senior Executive Officer
At Permanent Secretary level only

questions.hint: The SCS starts at Deputy Director.

questions.prompt: Who are non-executive directors on a departmental board?

options.text: Staff who represent the trade unions
Ministers who are also members of the Lords
Senior civil servants chosen by the Prime Minister from other departments
People from outside government who give advice and challenge

questions.hint: They are not civil servants.

questions.prompt: Which description fits where a new AO will normally work?

options.text: Directly under the Secretary of State
On the departmental board
In a team within a directorate and a group
In the Permanent Secretary's private office

questions.hint: AOs usually work in teams led by an EO or HEO.

questions.prompt: Which group of staff leads large groups of work below the Permanent Secretary?

options.text: Directors General
Non-executive directors
Private secretaries
Higher Executive Officers

questions.hint: Directors General lead large groups.

questions.prompt: Why does it help to understand your department's structure?

options.text: You can see who makes which decisions and who to ask
It tells you which ministers to vote for
It decides your pay, holiday entitlement and place on the grade ladder
It shows which departments to apply to

questions.hint: Understanding structure helps you navigate.

items.title: Executive agencies and arm's length bodies in practice (level 4)
items.source: GOV.UK, Departments, agencies and public bodies; Cabinet Office guidance
items.body: Executive agencies and arm's length bodies deliver much of what government does for the public, and they work in different ways. An executive agency is part of its parent department. Its staff are civil servants who work under a framework document agreed between the agency and the department. The framework sets out its aims, how it is governed and how it reports. A chief executive leads the agency and is accountable to the minister in the department. The minister still answers in Parliament for the agency. Examples are the DVLA, HM Passport Office and HM Prison and Probation Service. An arm's length body, also called a non-departmental public body or NDPB, is separate from its sponsor department. It may be created by law and have its own board. It is funded mostly by government but carries out its work at a distance from ministers, because independence is important to the job. Examples include the Environment Agency, the Care Quality Commission, the Health and Safety Executive and Arts Council England. The sponsor department sets the overall policy framework and oversees performance but does not direct day-to-day decisions. Staff in some arm's length bodies are civil servants, and others are employed under different rules. When you read a job advert, check who the employer is, because this decides the terms, the pension and whether the Civil Service Code applies.

questions.prompt: Who leads an executive agency and is accountable to the minister in the parent department?

options.text: A Permanent Secretary appointed to the agency
A chief executive appointed to run the agency
A board of non-executive directors acting alone
A Secretary of State assigned to the agency

questions.hint: Agencies are led by a chief executive.

questions.prompt: Who answers in Parliament for the work of an executive agency?

options.text: The Cabinet Secretary on the minister's behalf
The Speaker of the House of Commons
The minister in the parent department
The agency's chief executive in the Commons

questions.hint: The department's minister remains accountable.

questions.prompt: What does a framework document do for an agency?

options.text: Lists the names of all of the agency's current customers and their needs
Sets the pay for each of its individual staff
Records the agency's spending for each year
Sets out its aims, governance and how it reports

questions.hint: The framework document governs how the agency operates.

questions.prompt: What is another common name for an arm's length body?

options.text: A ministerial private office
A non-ministerial government department
A non-departmental public body
An executive agency

questions.hint: NDPB is the usual term.

questions.prompt: Why do some arm's length bodies work at a distance from ministers?

options.text: Independence matters for work such as regulation and inspection
Ministers have no legal power at all over how the body is funded
They are owned by private companies who pay for them
They are not accountable to anyone in government

questions.hint: Independence supports fair, credible decisions.

questions.prompt: What does the sponsor department do for an arm's length body?

options.text: Sets the overall policy framework and oversees performance
Employs all of the body's staff as civil servants
Takes over the role of the body's board
Makes the body's day-to-day operational decisions for its managers

questions.hint: The sponsor oversees without directing everyday decisions.

questions.prompt: Which of these is an arm's length body rather than an executive agency?

options.text: HM Land Registry
The Care Quality Commission
HM Passport Office
The Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency

questions.hint: The CQC is a non-departmental public body.

questions.prompt: Why should you check who the employer is in an advert from a public body?

options.text: It decides which grade you are allowed to apply for in the first year
It decides whether the job will involve ministers
It decides whether the post will be advertised in Wales
It decides your terms, your pension and whether the Code applies

questions.hint: Terms differ between employers.

items.title: Spending public money and value for money (level 4)
items.source: HM Treasury, Managing Public Money; National Audit Office
items.body: Public money is raised mainly through taxes, and government also borrows. The Treasury sets how much each department may spend. This is done in a Spending Review, which sets budgets for several years, and in annual estimates that Parliament votes on. Managing Public Money is the Treasury's guide that tells civil servants how to handle public funds properly. Its main principles are regularity, propriety, value for money and feasibility. Regularity means spending within the law and the limits Parliament has set. Propriety means meeting high standards of conduct, with fairness, honesty and avoidance of waste. Value for money is about getting the best result for the cost, which is judged by economy, efficiency and effectiveness. Economy means spending less to buy the same quality. Efficiency means getting more output for the same spending. Effectiveness means achieving the intended result. The National Audit Office (NAO) checks departmental accounts and reports on value for money to Parliament. Its head is the Comptroller and Auditor General. The Public Accounts Committee then questions senior civil servants about the NAO's findings. Day to day, these ideas show up in how civil servants buy goods and services through competition rather than favouring friends, keep receipts, claim only for genuine expenses, and report waste or error as soon as they find it.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of a Spending Review?

options.text: Deciding which ministers will lead each department
Checking the accounts of local councils in England
Voting on the salary of the Prime Minister each year
Setting departmental budgets for several years ahead

questions.hint: Spending Reviews set multi-year budgets.

questions.prompt: What does regularity mean in public spending?

options.text: Spending only on regular staff costs and not projects
Spending exactly the same amount of money in each month of the year
Spending money only in the final month of the year
Spending within the law and the limits Parliament has set

questions.hint: Regularity means lawful and authorised spending.

questions.prompt: Which of these best describes economy?

options.text: Achieving the result that the department intended in the first place
Spending less to buy goods or services of the same quality
Keeping the accounts accurate and up to date
Getting more output for the same level of spending

questions.hint: Economy is about lower input cost for the same quality.

questions.prompt: What does efficiency mean in value for money?

options.text: Choosing the cheapest supplier in every case
Spending less on staff than the department did in the year before
Meeting the target date for completing a project
Getting more output for the same level of spending

questions.hint: Efficiency compares output with spending.

questions.prompt: Who heads the National Audit Office?

options.text: The Cabinet Secretary
The Comptroller and Auditor General
The Chief Secretary to the Treasury
The Chancellor of the Exchequer

questions.hint: The Comptroller and Auditor General leads the NAO.

questions.prompt: Which parliamentary committee questions senior civil servants about the NAO's findings?

options.text: The Treasury Committee
The Liaison Committee
The Home Affairs Select Committee in the House of Commons
The Public Accounts Committee

questions.hint: The PAC follows up the NAO's reports.

questions.prompt: Which action by an AO fits the principles of Managing Public Money?

options.text: Buying from a friend's business without any competition
Keeping receipts and claiming only for genuine expenses
Rounding up expenses to the nearest pound for convenience
Using spare budget to buy equipment at the year end

questions.hint: Genuine claims show propriety.

questions.prompt: What should a civil servant do on finding that a payment has gone out in error?

options.text: Correct it quietly and tell nobody about it
Leave it for the auditors to find at year end
Wait to see whether the money is returned
Report it as soon as they find it

questions.hint: Reporting waste or error promptly is part of propriety.

items.title: Devolution and the civil servants who serve it (level 4)
items.source: GOV.UK, Devolution; Scottish Government; Welsh Government
items.body: Devolution means that some powers have been passed from the UK Parliament to the Scottish Parliament, the Senedd Cymru (Welsh Parliament) and the Northern Ireland Assembly. These bodies make laws and decisions on devolved matters, which include health, education, and many aspects of transport and housing. Reserved or excepted matters, such as defence, foreign affairs and most of tax and benefits, stay with the UK government and Parliament, although details differ between nations. Scottish Government and Welsh Government staff are civil servants who serve the devolved ministers. They are members of the Home Civil Service, and they follow the Civil Service Code. The Northern Ireland Civil Service is a separate service, with its own recruitment, grades and rules, serving the Northern Ireland Executive. Civil servants in UK government departments, such as DWP and HMRC, work in all four nations, delivering UK-wide services. Civil servants may work across both UK and devolved government at times, for example on shared problems such as health or the economy. In Wales, the Welsh language is important, and some jobs ask for Welsh skills. Because devolution has made the picture more complex, the Cabinet Office and devolved governments work together to coordinate matters that affect more than one nation. If you apply to a devolved government, use its own recruitment pages and read the advert for the terms.

questions.prompt: Which area is normally a devolved matter?

options.text: Most of the benefits system
Health
Foreign affairs
Defence

questions.hint: Health is devolved to the nations.

questions.prompt: Which area is normally reserved to the UK government?

options.text: Defence
Health
Housing
Education

questions.hint: Defence stays with the UK government.

questions.prompt: Whom do Scottish Government civil servants serve?

options.text: The councillors of Scotland's local councils
The Presiding Officer of the Scottish Parliament
Only the Prime Minister in Westminster
The devolved Scottish ministers

questions.hint: They serve the devolved ministers.

questions.prompt: Which body is part of the devolved structure of the UK?

options.text: The Senedd Cymru
The House of Lords
The Cabinet Office
The Supreme Court

questions.hint: The Senedd is the Welsh Parliament.

questions.prompt: How does the Northern Ireland Civil Service differ from the Scottish and Welsh Government civil services?

options.text: It is run directly by the UK Cabinet Office in London
It is a separate civil service with its own rules
It has no grade structure of its own
It is not covered by any code of conduct

questions.hint: NICS is separate from the Home Civil Service.

questions.prompt: Which statement about UK departments such as DWP and HMRC is correct?

options.text: They work only in the nations where the department has its own minister
They deliver UK-wide services with staff in all four nations
They were replaced by devolved bodies in each nation
They operate only in London and the south east

questions.hint: Large UK departments have offices across the UK.

questions.prompt: Why do the Cabinet Office and devolved governments work together?

options.text: To set the same pay for staff in each nation
To coordinate matters that affect more than one nation
To combine all of the civil services into one
To stop the devolved governments from making laws in their own areas

questions.hint: Coordination is needed on shared issues.

questions.prompt: Where should you apply for a job in the Welsh Government?

options.text: Through the Welsh Government's own recruitment pages
Through the Northern Ireland Civil Service pages only
Through the Cabinet Office's pages only
Through the Scottish Government's recruitment pages

questions.hint: Each government recruits through its own pages.

items.title: Moving up: how promotion works in practice (level 4)
items.body: Promotion in the Civil Service is based on merit. There is no automatic promotion because of time served. To move up, a person normally applies for a vacancy at the next grade, in their own department or elsewhere, and is assessed in the same way as an outside applicant, using Success Profiles. This usually means showing behaviours and experience at the next level, and sometimes strengths, ability or technical skills. The Civil Service Behaviours are described at different levels, so an application for EO would be assessed on the level for that grade. Evidence of what you have done matters, so keep a record of tasks you have led, problems you have solved and feedback you have received. Some routes help you gain this evidence. Temporary promotion means doing a higher-grade job for a fixed period. A loan or secondment means working in another team, department or organisation for a time. Shadowing means observing someone in a job you are interested in. Many departments run development schemes aimed at helping lower-grade staff move up. Regular one-to-ones with your line manager, and an annual performance review, give a record of how you are doing. If you do not succeed, ask for feedback. It is a normal part of the process, and it helps you to improve your next application. Moving between departments can also widen your experience and open new options.

questions.prompt: How does promotion normally happen in the Civil Service?

options.text: By recommendation from a minister who knows your work
By applying for a vacancy at the next grade and being assessed on merit
By being nominated by a trade union representative
By moving up automatically after serving a set number of years in a grade

questions.hint: Promotion is competitive and merit-based.

questions.prompt: Which framework is used to assess applications for promotion?

items.title: Diversity, inclusion and staff networks (level 4)
items.source: Civil Service Diversity and Inclusion Strategy; Equality Act 2010
items.body: The Civil Service aims to reflect the people it serves. It wants staff from all backgrounds, so that its policies and services work for everyone. Diversity means having a mix of people with different backgrounds, ages, ethnicities, abilities and experiences. Inclusion means making sure everyone can take part and be heard and feel they belong. The Equality Act 2010 protects people from discrimination on nine protected characteristics, and the Public Sector Equality Duty requires public bodies to think about equality in their decisions. The Civil Service has also set out its own approach in a diversity and inclusion strategy. Departments run staff networks, which are groups for people who share an experience or characteristic, such as disability, race, faith, gender, age or being a carer. They offer support, social contact and a voice to management. Anyone can usually join as a member or ally. The Disability Confident scheme offers an interview to disabled candidates who meet the minimum criteria for a job. Reasonable adjustments in recruitment and at work remove barriers, and may include extra time in tests, adjustable equipment or a different way of working. Staff are expected to treat colleagues and customers with respect. Bullying, harassment and discrimination break the Civil Service Code and can lead to disciplinary action. If you see or experience unacceptable behaviour, you can report it to your manager, HR or the nominated officer.

items.title: Serving customers well (level 4)
items.source: GOV.UK, Service Standard; Civil Service Code
items.body: Much of the work done by Administrative Officers is serving the public, so the quality of service matters. The Civil Service Code says civil servants must deal with the public and their affairs fairly, efficiently, promptly, effectively and sensitively. In practice, this starts with listening. Let the person explain, check you have understood by repeating back the main points, and stay calm even if they are upset. Use plain English and avoid jargon or abbreviations the customer will not know. Explain what will happen next and how long it will take, and do what you say you will. If you cannot help, say so honestly and point the customer to someone who can. Customers who are vulnerable, for example because of ill health, bereavement, language difficulty or money worries, may need extra care, patience and time. Some may need information in a different format. Never make promises you cannot keep, and never give advice that is outside your role. Be careful to confirm who you are speaking to before you share any personal information. Departments use set security questions to do this. If someone is abusive, follow the department's policy, which may include ending the contact. Keep clear notes of each conversation, because someone else may need to pick up the case later. When mistakes happen, apologise, put them right and learn from them.

items.title: Handling information: classification and sharing (level 4)
items.source: GOV.UK, Government Security Classifications; Data Protection Act 2018
items.body: Good information handling combines the security classifications with the rules on personal data. Most government information is classed as OFFICIAL, but this does not mean it can be shared freely. Some of it is marked OFFICIAL-SENSITIVE because losing it could cause more damage, for example personal data about many people, or commercial information. The principle of need to know applies: you should only see and share information that you need for your work. When sharing, use approved channels such as the department's email and secure file systems, and check the recipient's address carefully before sending. Personal email, text messages, social media and unapproved cloud storage should not be used for work information. When you work from home, keep work papers and devices out of sight, do not let others use your equipment, and avoid working in public places where a screen can be seen. Dispose of paper with personal data in the secure confidential waste bins, not in the ordinary bin. Do not leave papers on printers. Report any suspected loss, theft or wrongful disclosure at once, even if you think it is small, because delay makes damage worse and departments have legal duties to report serious breaches to the Information Commissioner's Office within a short time limit. Mistakes happen and are treated sympathetically when reported quickly. Hiding them is treated far more seriously.

items.title: Working in a team: roles and expectations (level 4)
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles; Civil Service Jobs
items.body: Most civil servants work in a team, and the way a team works affects how well the service runs. A team in an operational delivery setting may have a team leader, often an EO or HEO, a group of AOs and AAs who do the day-to-day work, and sometimes specialists who handle complex cases. The team leader allocates work, supports staff, checks quality, and handles problems that others cannot. Team members are expected to work to standards and deadlines, record their work accurately, share knowledge, and ask for help when needed. Handover is a key skill. When you pass a case to a colleague, write clear notes so they can carry on without calling the customer to start again. Good teams share workload fairly, tell each other about problems early, and treat each other with respect. In a one-to-one, a manager reviews your work, sets objectives, and discusses wellbeing and development. Objectives should be clear and measurable, such as completing a number of cases at a set accuracy level. Quality checks, sometimes called assurance, sample a few of your cases to confirm they are right. These are normal, and are meant to help you learn. If you disagree with feedback, ask for an example and discuss it calmly. The Success Profiles behaviour Working Together covers these skills, and employers look for examples of helping colleagues and sharing information.

items.title: Starting at AO: what to expect and how to learn (level 4)
items.source: Civil Service Jobs; GOV.UK, Civil Service Learning
items.body: Your first weeks as an Administrative Officer follow a pattern. Before you start you receive a contract and your confirmed start date once the pre-employment checks are cleared. On the first day you meet your line manager and team, receive equipment and a pass, and attend an induction. Over the following weeks you complete mandatory learning, covering topics such as the Civil Service Code, security, data protection, equality and fire safety. You also learn the systems and rules for the particular work, often with a mix of classroom or online training and supervised practice. At first your cases may be checked closely, and you may be given simpler cases before more complex ones. This is normal and nobody expects you to know everything. A probation period applies in many departments, and your manager will review progress during it. Use your one-to-ones to ask questions, flag anything you find difficult and discuss training. Keep your own notes of what you learn. Treat guidance documents as the source of truth, and when you are unsure, check the guidance or ask rather than guess. Over time you will become faster and more confident. Learning does not stop after induction, as departments offer online courses, workshops and coaching, and you can build a personal development plan with your manager to prepare for promotion.
